candidates.name: Kohaku
candidates.reason: 3-star innovative kaiseki, deep-verified for reputation and price, but no source confirmed private-room capacity for 6 and the restaurant's own site was blocked to fetch — real booking-window risk this close to Sept/Oct at 7.5 weeks out. Kept as a lead for a future pass rather than shipped.

candidates.name: Aragawa
candidates.reason: Independent critics rank it among the best steak experiences in Japan, categorically different from the wagyu/kaiseki finalists — but the ~22-seat total restaurant size (press estimate, not an official figure) makes a same-night table of 6 a real risk. Preserved as Worth the Effort rather than the primary anchor.

candidates.name: Sazenka
candidates.reason: 2-star Japanese-Chinese fusion; private room capacity is 2-6, exactly fitting the party, and online TableCheck booking exists — but the 2-month phone booking window is already open/closing as of this pass, and the Oct 17 dinner would land on the Shanghai-crab seasonal menu rather than the more-reviewed standard course. Kept as a lead, not shipped as primary or fallback given RyuGin/Ukai-tei cover the anchor + safety-net roles already.

candidates.name: Sukiyabashi Jiro
candidates.reason: Delisted from Michelin, no longer accepts general public reservations; ~10-seat counter, foreigners generally need an existing relationship via a Japanese host/concierge. Unbookable for 6 unrelated guests on this timeline.

candidates.name: Sushi Saito
candidates.reason: Booking gated behind Pocket Concierge + Amex Platinum-or-higher card ownership; 8-10 seat counter. As hard to secure as Jiro, and the card-gating alone rules out a general party booking.

candidates.name: Sushi Yoshitake
candidates.reason: No confirmed group-of-6 booking path found; small-counter format typical of this tier makes 6 unlikely.

candidates.name: Sushi Kanda
candidates.reason: No reservation or foreigner-access information surfaced at all in discovery.

candidates.name: Sushi Masashi
candidates.reason: 9-seat counter plus a private room for only 4 — cannot seat 6 in one sitting.

candidates.name: Florilège
candidates.reason: Multiple sources confirm a max party size of 4 guests — cannot seat 6.

candidates.name: L'Effervescence
candidates.reason: 3-star; no group-of-6 capacity data found in discovery-level searches. Not deep-verified given stronger confirmed alternatives — a candidate for a future pass.

candidates.name: Narisawa
candidates.reason: Reputation for extreme booking difficulty confirmed at discovery level; no capacity/group data found. Not deep-verified.

candidates.name: Den
candidates.reason: Phone-only booking up to 2 months ahead, widely described as an 'impossible reservation'; no confirmed seating capacity for 6 found — too much unquantified risk for a single-shot anchor.

candidates.name: Kadowaki
candidates.reason: 3-star; surfaced only in passing (20 total seats, 6 at counter). Not deep-verified.

candidates.name: Ishikawa
candidates.reason: 3-star; surfaced only as a name in discovery. Not deep-verified.

candidates.name: Wagyu Yakiniku Isshin
candidates.reason: Surfaced at discovery level; not deep-verified given Ushigoro already covers the self-booked group yakiniku slot.

candidates.name: Inakaya
candidates.reason: Fun, theatrical robatayaki, well-reviewed for groups, but priced and positioned as a boisterous crowd-pleaser (¥8,000-10,000) rather than a quality-ceiling showcase — doesn't meet the anchor's 'quality difference is material' bar.

candidates.name: Gonpachi
candidates.reason: Legitimately decent, authentic-enough food, but consistently described by reviewers as tourist-oriented with inconsistent service relative to price. Fine for a casual night, not the anchor.

candidates.name: Unotoki
candidates.reason: Only 16 total seats (6 counter + ~5 per private room) — too small to confidently fit 6 in one seating.

candidates.name: Tempura Kondo
candidates.reason: Counter-format restaurants of this style are almost always small-capacity; no group-of-6 data found, not pursued given diminishing returns.

candidates.name: teamLab Borderless
candidates.reason: Legitimate alternative to Planets, but not shipped given light-touch sights scope for a food-priority trip — Planets pairs geographically with Toyosu Market, this doesn't pair as cleanly with a food stop.

candidates.name: Tokyo Skytree
candidates.reason: More expensive (¥1,800-3,100 vs Tokyo Tower's ¥1,500) and, per multiple comparisons, the 450m deck makes landmarks read as miniatures — a worse trade for a group not prioritizing sightseeing. Tokyo Tower shipped instead.

candidates.name: Shibuya Crossing
candidates.reason: No admission/content beyond a photo op; light-touch sights scope favored food-adjacent stops (Yanaka Ginza, Asakusa) over a pass-through landmark.

candidates.name: Akihabara
candidates.reason: Pop-culture district with a real food identity (ramen, Michelin-listed tempura/soba), but not deep-verified or shipped given the guide's light-touch sights budget was already spent on stronger food-adjacent picks.

candidates.name: Kura Sushi
candidates.reason: World's largest kaiten-zushi (277 capacity), genuinely group-of-6 capable — but Uobei Shibuya already covers the easy-arrival-night sushi slot without duplicating the pick. Kept as a lead for a future pass or a Skytree-area day.

candidates.name: Sushi Dai
candidates.reason: ≈12-seat counter, 2-5 hour waits, sells out by 9-11am — would force a party of 6 to split into separate seatings. Routed around explicitly in the guide's Toyosu day.

candidates.name: Daiwa Sushi
candidates.reason: Larger than Sushi Dai (~40 seats) but still a single shared counter with multi-hour waits — same group-splitting problem.

candidates.name: Uogashi Nihon-Ichi
candidates.reason: Standing sushi bar chain with only 6-7 total standing spots per branch, no seating — workable for 2, not a party of 6 eating together.

candidates.name: Gyutan Iroha
candidates.reason: Legitimate group-bookable alternative to Torien in the same alley (organizer-free-of-charge deal for parties of 5+) — Torien shipped instead since it was verified first and covers the same need.

candidates.name: Tsukishima Meibutsu Monja Daruma
candidates.reason: Monjayaki is a genuinely Tokyo-local specialty most first-timer guides miss, and the format suits a group of 6 — but posted hours couldn't be reconciled between two sources (10:30-22:30 vs 11:30/11:00-23:00) to the standard this guide holds for a shipped fact. Not shipped; a good lead for a follow-up pass.

candidates.name: Fuunji
candidates.reason: Small-counter tsukemen shop, 45-90 min queues at peak; a party of 6 walking in together won't be seated together. Poor group fit despite strong reputation.

candidates.name: Tatsunoya
candidates.reason: Small-counter tonkotsu shop with near-constant queues — a group of 6 would likely be seated in shifts, working against the low-friction brief.

candidates.name: Rokurinsha
candidates.reason: Near-constant 30-45+ minute queue at all hours — tourist-trap-adjacent given the wait-to-quality ratio for a group this size.

candidates.name: Ichiran
candidates.reason: Individual solo-booth design defeats the point of a group meal — fine for a solo traveler, poor fit as this party's ramen night.

candidates.name: Afuri
candidates.reason: Most branches are counter-only and small (the original Ebisu branch has 9 seats); even the larger Nakameguro branch is tight for 6.

candidates.name: Kanda Yabu Soba
candidates.reason: Historic (1880) soba house that explicitly takes group reservations on its 2F course menu, unlike most soba counters — genuinely workable for 6, but not shipped since the day plan's food slots were already filled by stronger, more distinct picks.

candidates.name: Tempura Tsunahachi
candidates.reason: No explicit group-seating information found; moderate risk for 6 walking in at peak. Not deep-verified further given other picks already covered Shinjuku.

candidates.name: Maisen Tonkatsu
candidates.reason: No-reservation walk-in only, larger space than a typical counter shop (former bathhouse) — a reasonable lead, not deep-verified for group wait times.

candidates.name: Tendon Tenya
candidates.reason: Reliable no-fuss chain backup (130+ locations, no line culture) — not shipped as a named day-plan stop since the itinerary's meals were already covered, but worth knowing about as a fallback.

candidates.name: Isetan Shinjuku
candidates.reason: Strong depachika (basement food hall) option for an independent-grazing lunch — not shipped as a named stop given the day plan's meals were already set, a good flex option if plans change.

candidates.name: Mitsukoshi Ginza
candidates.reason: Alternative depachika near the Ginza dinner venues — not shipped as a named stop, same reasoning as Isetan Shinjuku.

candidates.name: Café de l'Ambre
candidates.reason: Historic kissaten (since 1948) with genuine café-culture credibility, but small/traditional seating is a poor fit for a party of 6 as a single stop — not shipped.

candidates.name: Fuji Soba
candidates.reason: Standing-soba chain, genuinely the lowest-friction Tokyo breakfast format (ticket machine, stand-and-eat) — not shipped as a named day-plan stop since it works anywhere, mentioned as a category rather than a single pick.

candidates.name: Kobikicho Ohno
candidates.reason: Pass B's independently-found anchor candidate (native-language-only discovery) — a tea-kaiseki restaurant serving a single reservation a day, sole private room fits 6 exactly with zero overflow buffer. Genuinely exceptional and distinct from RyuGin, but RyuGin already has a confirmed concierge booking route and buffer capacity to 8 — reconciled as a Worth-the-Effort alternative rather than replacing RyuGin as the anchor, per the intake's own instruction to preserve rather than silently drop an exceptional-but-inconvenient option.

candidates.name: Koumoto
candidates.reason: Pass B's second native-only find — soba-kappo restaurant with confirmed foreign-card acceptance and flexible private-room capacity to 8, genuinely solid. Not shipped: Ginza Ukai-tei already covers the self-service, no-concierge fallback role and Kobikicho Ohno covers the Worth-the-Effort alternative role, so adding a third Saturday-dinner-tier option would dilute rather than strengthen the section. Kept as a lead for a future pass.

candidates.name: Narukiyo
candidates.reason: Pass B (own rejection, carried across unchanged): kitchen-facing seating is a standing-style counter, unsuited to a seated 6-person dinner; already surfaced in English-language tourist guides (Tabelog EN, Time Out Tokyo), undermining the under-the-radar angle; phone line found closed at time of research.

candidates.name: Kagayaki
candidates.reason: Pass B (own rejection, carried across unchanged): all-you-can-eat yakiniku/shabu-shabu buffet format — a value/quantity pick, not the quality-led anchor experience the trip's food priority calls for.

candidates.name: Miyabi
candidates.reason: Pass B (own rejection, carried across unchanged): surfaced from a single blog only, a generic high-end Roppongi tourist-district spot without a distinct local angle — dropped once Ohno/Koumoto proved stronger, better-corroborated picks.

candidates.name: Kaigen
candidates.reason: Pass B (own rejection, carried across unchanged): appealing insider tuna-bowl pick inside Tsukiji Outer Market, but only one current (≤24-month) independent firsthand account exists — the other two corroborating accounts are from 2022, past the experiential-freshness bar. Worth re-checking with a fresh search in a later pass.

evidence.claim: Private Room 1 seats 6-8 guests; Private Room 2 seats 5-8. Restaurant is 40 seats total, no counter.

Phone-only reservations (+81-3-3423-8006, 11:30-18:00); overseas guests must book through a Tokyo hotel concierge or an approved partner (e.g. My Concierge Japan / OMAKASE) — no direct self-service booking for foreign guests. Following month's reservations open the 1st of the current month, so October dates open Sept 1, 2026.
¥70,000/person course + 15% service charge in private rooms. No-show/same-day cancellation is ¥20,000 per absent guest; must reconfirm by phone the day before by 18:00. Minimum age 10.

Currently holds 3 Michelin stars. Discovery-level search (not independently confirmed via this fetch) suggested the streak runs 15 consecutive years since 2012 — the 3-star status itself is fetched-confirmed, the exact streak length is a secondary, less-certain detail.

Self-service online booking via TableCheck, no concierge dependency. Grand Courses ¥27,500 or ¥38,500/person (tax incl.) + 13% service charge; Kobe A5 upgrade +¥17,000/person. Minimum 2 people per course. Dinner last order 19:30, kitchen closes 21:30. Closed Sundays + 2 Mondays/month.
Cancellation: 50% fee if cancelled 1 day prior, 100% same-day (set course); seating-only cancellation ¥15,000/person (1 day prior), ¥30,000/person (same-day).
Repeatedly cited by independent food critics (Andy Hayler, Spear's magazine) as one of the most extraordinary steak experiences in Japan; charcoal-grilled Tajima-lineage beef, founded 1967.
Repeatedly cited by independent food critics as one of the most extraordinary steak experiences in Japan.
Total restaurant capacity is reported at only ≈22 seats — a secondhand press/blog estimate, not an official Aragawa-published figure. Aragawa's own site could not be reached to confirm.
The dining area seats up to 22 guests — an intimate setting, unchanged in design since the restaurant's 1967 founding.

Booking via TableCheck; credit card required to reserve. October seasonal 'long-term farmed Tajima beef' course ¥60,500/person (service excl., tax incl.) + 12% service charge; minimum order 2 people. Cancellation: 50% within 48 hours, 100% within 24 hours or no-show, charged automatically.
Reservations accepted for 1 to 8 people via online TableCheck booking; the S. Ginza branch has 11 private rooms.
Private room capacity is 2-6 guests (minimum 4) across three private rooms on two floors, plus a main dining hall. TableCheck's party-size selector explicitly offers 1-6.

3 Michelin stars in the 2025/2026 Michelin Guide; relocated to Kagurazaka April 2024. Counter seats described as always fully booked; private room is the practical route for a group, exact capacity not published anywhere found.
US passport holders are visa-exempt for tourism stays up to 90 days; no current ETA/pre-authorization is required for entry.

Japan's planned ETA-style Electronic Travel Authorization (JESTA) passed the Diet in 2026 but implementation targets FY2028 (by March 31, 2029) via a future phased rollout — it will not affect an Oct 2026 trip.

mofa.go.jp (the authoritative source for Japan visa-exemption policy) refuses automated fetch (HTTP 403) — verified against a reference (JNTO) source instead; recommend a manual recheck before departure.

travel.state.gov refuses automated fetch (HTTP 403, Cloudflare-gated) — the current advisory level could not be independently verified this pass. A search-preview snippet suggests Level 1, but that is not promoted to a shipped fact.
Tipping is not customary in restaurants, bars, cafes, taxis, or hotels; leaving cash on the table causes confusion and staff may try to return it.

Otoshi (small unrequested appetizer, a few hundred yen/person) is standard izakaya practice and appears on the bill regardless of consumption; chopstick etiquette (never upright in rice, never pass chopstick-to-chopstick); shoes off on tatami seating.

Seven Bank ATMs: 24/7, 28,000+ locations at 7-Eleven stores nationwide, accept Visa/Plus, Mastercard/Maestro/Cirrus, UnionPay, Amex, JCB, Discover, Diners Club. Per-withdrawal limit for overseas-issued cards is ¥100,000 (¥30,000 for magnetic-stripe-only cards).

Tourist PASMO: ¥1,000-¥10,000 depending on purchase point, valid 28 days from purchase, no deposit, balance not refundable. Sold at Haneda (Keikyu counters/machines) and Narita (Keisei info centers, ¥2,000 card). Launched May 20, 2026.
Keisei Skyliner: non-stop Narita to Nippori (~36-41 min) or Ueno (~41 min); one-way fare ≈¥2,470.
Tokyo Monorail: Haneda to Hamamatsucho as fast as 13 min. Keikyu Line: Haneda to Shinagawa in 11-14 min depending on terminal, through-runs onto Toei Asakusa Line.

Japan's tax-free shopping system switches from instant point-of-sale exemption to a refund-at-departure system for purchases made on or after November 1, 2026 (refunds within 90 days of purchase, via customs inspection at departure). The Oct 16-20, 2026 trip falls entirely before this cutover, so the traveler will experience the old instant-discount system.
No Japanese national holiday falls within Oct 16-20, 2026 — nearest is Sports Day (Oct 12) before the trip and Culture Day (Nov 3) after.
Free entry; main hall open 6:00 AM-5:00 PM (6:30 AM Oct-Mar).
Grounds free; gate hours track sunrise/sunset (roughly 5:00 AM-6:40 PM depending on season). Museum ¥1,000 adult, closed Thursdays.
Weekday early morning (≈7 AM) is genuinely quiet — a few hundred visitors versus tens of thousands by midday.
Coming super early in the morning gives a tranquil, peaceful experience before the crowds build.
The shrine's forest is not old-growth — it was deliberately planted from barren grassland starting in 1915, designed to read as an ancient forest after ~150 years.
≈¥3,800 weekday / ¥4,200 weekend adult, timed entry.

The original teamLab Borderless in Odaiba is closed (the official site's own heading reads 'teamLab Borderless Odaiba (Closed)'); it reopened at Azabudai Hills in February 2024 per discovery-level search.
Oct 1-Mar 14 hours: 9:00 AM-4:30 PM, last entry 4:00 PM. Adults ¥500. Closed every Monday (or the following weekday if Monday is a holiday).
Main Deck admission from ¥1,500, opens 9:00 AM.
The wholesale market and tuna auction relocated to Toyosu in October 2018. Tsukiji's Outer Market (food stalls/restaurants) never closed and remains open.

Toyosu tuna auction viewing ≈5:30-6:30 AM; market open 5 AM-5 PM; closed Sundays and most Wednesdays plus public holidays. The Tokyo Metropolitan Central Wholesale Market publishes an exact 2026 calendar, but its daily grid was not machine-readable this pass — exact October closure dates need a closer-to-trip recheck.
8-9 AM has stalls fully stocked with manageable crowds; 10 AM-12 PM is peak with 30-60 min lines at famous stalls.
9 AM-1 PM is the peak crowd window at Tsukiji Outer Market.
Sushi Dai routinely runs 2-5 hour waits and sells out by 9-11am on busy days.
Multi-hour waits are standard at Sushi Dai even on an early-morning visit.

Sushi Dai has ≈12 counter seats; Daiwa Sushi is larger (≈40) but still a single shared counter — a party of 6 would very likely split into two groups seated separately. Secondhand estimate (no official seat count published), corroborated by the independent multi-hour-wait accounts above which are consistent with a very small room.

150 total seats, floor rentals available for 30+ people — a party of 6 is a normal booking, not an edge case. Hours: Mon-Thu/Sun/holidays 11:30-23:30, Fri-Sat 11:30-23:45 (food last order 23:00); closed only New Year's Day. Bookable via Hot Pepper Gourmet.
Weekday mornings after 11 AM and Tue-Thu are calmest at Ameya-Yokocho; weekends and evenings after 6 PM get packed.
Morning visits before the weekend crowds build are the best time to see Ameyoko functioning as a real shopping street.

The Japan Meteorological Corporation had not yet published a 2026 autumn-foliage (koyo) forecast as of this pass — the last published forecast (for the 2025 season) put Tokyo's peak at Nov 27 (yellow) / Dec 2 (red), a prior-year lead only. Either way, the Oct 16-20, 2026 trip sits well before any plausible Tokyo koyo window.
Kobikicho Ohno (木挽町 大野), a tea-kaiseki restaurant in Yotsuya-sanchome, accepts only one reservation/party per day — the entire restaurant serves a single seating.

Official site lists dinner hours 17:00–21:00 (drinks last order 20:00), with no fixed weekly closure day but irregular ad-hoc closures ('定休日なし（不定休日あり）'); Saturday hours are not separately differentiated on the site, so confirm directly for a specific date.
The restaurant's only private room (horigotatsu sunken-hearth, with door and walls) seats 2–6 guests — a party of 6 fills it exactly, with no overflow buffer for a 7th guest.
≈¥15,000 per person average budget for dinner, per Gurunavi's operator listing (the restaurant's own official site does not publish a fixed course price).
Cancellation fee tiers per Gurunavi's operator listing: 50% fee inside 7 days of the reservation date, full charge inside 3 days.

Official site states an English-language menu and English-speaking staff are available; card acceptance is not mentioned on the official site or the Gurunavi operator page — unconfirmed, ask when booking.
Koumoto (こうもと), a soba-kappo restaurant in Nishi-Azabu/Minami-Azabu, is open Saturdays 17:00–22:00 (food last order 21:00, drinks last order 21:30), per its HotPepper Gourmet operator page.
Two 2nd-floor private rooms (seating 2–4 and 3–8) plus additional 3rd-floor rooms, combinable up to 12 guests — comfortably fits a party of 6 with spare capacity, unlike Ohno's exact-fit room.
≈¥10,000 per person starting price for dinner courses, plus a 10% service charge, per HotPepper's operator listing.
Accepts Visa, Mastercard, Diners Club, and JCB — confirmed foreign-card compatibility, stronger than Kobikicho Ohno's (unconfirmed).

Tsukiji Outer Market is markedly less crowded in the early morning (roughly before 9:00–9:30am) and crowding concentrates in specific hotspot areas rather than across the whole market; Wednesdays and Sundays see reduced stall operations (only about half the shops open).

disagreements.topic: Whether Sazenka's Oct 12, 2026 menu-listing cutoff signals a closure or a seasonal menu change
disagreements.investigation: An initial search result implying the regular course 'ends Oct 12' looked like a possible closure risk for an Oct 17 dinner. A follow-up search found the restaurant shifts to a Shanghai-crab-focused seasonal course from Oct 13, 2026 through Jan 16, 2027 — a menu changeover, not a closure. Not investigated further since Sazenka wasn't shipped as primary/fallback.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed as a seasonal menu changeover; an Oct 17 dinner at Sazenka would be on the crab-season menu, a different but not lesser experience than most published reviews describe.

disagreements.topic: Ginza Ukai-tei's price — an aggregator quoted '$250-600 per couple' while the restaurant's own site lists per-person course prices

saturation.note: Merged across both passes. Pass A's ~24-candidate anchor-dinner sweep (English-language, official/operator sources) and Pass B's independent native-language sweep (Japanese reservation-difficulty/capacity vocabulary) converged on complementary, non-overlapping candidate sets rather than a factual conflict: Pass A's RyuGin/Ukai-tei/Aragawa are internationally-known, deepest-documented picks; Pass B's Kobikicho Ohno/Koumoto are genuinely under-the-radar, native-only-discoverable finds, with Narukiyo/Kagayaki/Miyabi/Kaigen rejected within Pass B's own funnel. Reconciled by ROLE, not by disproof: RyuGin ships as the anchor (best-documented booking route + 6–8 buffer capacity), Kobikicho Ohno is adopted as an additional Worth-the-Effort alternative (single-seating-per-day exclusivity, exact-fit-6 capacity), Koumoto stays shortlisted-not-shipped (solid but redundant with Ukai-tei's fallback role). Tsukiji Outer Market's crowd timing was independently corroborated by both passes — Pass B's two fetched (not search-preview) Japanese-language firsthand accounts additionally confirmed a Wednesday reduced-stall pattern alongside the Sunday one Pass A had already found, folded into the guide. Casual-food discovery (Pass A) covered markets, ramen, sushi formats, izakaya, tempura/tonkatsu, depachika, café culture and a local specialty (monjayaki) across ~28 named candidates before the English-language pool was exhausted; sights discovery covered the standard marquee set plus corrections (Tsukiji/Toyosu, teamLab relocation, Meiji Jingu forest). No unresolved evidence from either pass would change the shipped anchor, fallback, or detour set — remaining open threads (Kohaku/Sazenka booking-route confirmation, Ohno's exact Saturday availability, Monja Daruma's hours, Toyosu's live October calendar) are pre-trip rechecks, not discovery gaps.

nativeLanguage.why: English/generic search results for 'Tokyo restaurant for 6' or 'best Tokyo izakaya' are dominated by SEO round-ups (ikyu.com, hitosara.com, Retty, Tabelog matome pages) and don't surface exclusive, reservation-hard venues. Japanese queries built around reservation-difficulty and room-capacity vocabulary (予約困難, 個室6名, 隠れ家, 一軒家) reached restaurants with little to no English coverage, matching the anti-default charter; yt-dlp is not installed in this environment, so the video-transcript lead channel was skipped per the bot-blocked doctrine and did not block the pass.

nativeLanguage.yield: Surfaced two non-default anchor-dinner candidates confirmed (via fetched operator/official sources) to fit a party of 6 in a private room: Kobikicho Ohno (one-party-per-day tea-kaiseki, exact 6-seat room) and Koumoto (soba-kappo, private rooms to 8, confirmed card acceptance). Corroborated Tsukiji Outer Market's early-morning off-peak window from two independent firsthand blogs. Identified and rejected three candidates that looked promising but didn't clear the bar: Narukiyo (standing-counter format wrong for a seated 6-top, and already English-tourist-discovered), Kagayaki (all-you-can-eat format mismatched to the quality-first brief), and Kaigen (appealing insider tuna-bowl pick, but its only current firsthand corroboration is a single 2025 source — the other two are 2022, past the 24-month freshness bar).
